title: Not more books
hookLine: progress isn't reading more, it's how you desire and avoid (Discourses 1.4)

lines: TEST ME, I'VE READ IT ALL.
cards: There's a stack of books by your bed, or a list of podcasts, or forty saved articles about becoming calmer. Finishing them can look like progress. A student in Epictetus' classroom felt the same way.
He walked up holding a scroll by Chrysippus, the great Stoic writer, and said, more or less: look how well I've read it. He expected praise. What he got was a put-down borrowed from the gym.

teach.h: THE ATHLETE'S SHOULDERS, NOT HIS WEIGHTS.
teach.b: This is Discourses book one, chapter four, on progress.
Imagine asking an athlete to show you his shoulders, Epictetus says, and he answers: look at my weights. Wonderful weights. I wanted to see what they did to you.
The scroll is the weights. Reading it is the lifting. Progress is what changes in you.
And he's precise about where to look. Show me your desire and your aversion: do you still want things that aren't in your power, and dread things you can't avoid?
Show me how you act: do you choose and refuse with care, or on impulse? Show me how you judge: do you agree to every impression that shows up, or do you check it? That's where progress lives.
He isn't against books; he respects Chrysippus as a guide. A map is worth having.
But a map isn't the trip. You can know the whole route to a city and never leave your chair.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO DOESN'T SNAP ANYMORE.
teach.b: Epictetus wants to see someone who used to snap at their brother and doesn't anymore, someone who used to panic at bad news and now takes a breath.
That person may have read less than the student with the scroll, and traveled further.
It's a little uncomfortable, because reading is pleasant and safe, and the other kind of progress happens in traffic, at dinner, in the middle of an argument.
But that's exactly where Epictetus sends his students, and that's where he'd come looking for them.

how: Some readers of the Stoics keep a short evening review of how they reacted that day, treating reading as preparation and changed reactions as the real measure.

o: progress, seen in how you desire, act and judge
a calm that comes once you've finished studying
progress, measured by how much you've read

games.q: progress, Epictetus' way: tap the pairs.
p: what the training did to you
how you desire, act and judge

s: Epictetus tells his students to stop reading Chrysippus
he values Chrysippus as a guide; he just says reading isn't the progress.
he compares a proud reader to an athlete showing off his weights
he wanted to see the shoulders, not the weights.
for Epictetus, progress shows up in what you want and avoid
desire and aversion come first in his list, then action and judgment.

games.q: a student hands Epictetus a scroll and says: test me, I've read it all. what does Epictetus do?
o: asks to see what the reading has changed in him.
games.why: he says it's like an athlete showing his weights: show me the shoulders, show me your desires and judgments.

practice: Pick one reaction you'd like to change: the flash of irritation in traffic, the sinking feeling at an email, the urge to check your phone.
Think back a year and ask whether it was stronger then, or the same, measuring the way an athlete checks one lift, without grading yourself. Then rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Prokopē, the Greek word for progress: not how much you've read, but how you now desire, act and judge. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek prokopē: progress, moving forward; the title word of Discourses 1.4.

carryVoice: Your line: show me how you act. The shoulders, not the weights. That's day three hundred ninety-four.
